credit.authors: Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, Omar Khattab (MIT CSAIL)
credit.title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights

ncm_credit.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation

trackA.title: Bionic circuits: an exact adder written into Qwen2.5-0.5B
trackA.test: 960 hidden problems a+b=, 1-12 digits, 4 prompt formats (2 unseen), greedy, exact match; guard = perplexity and next-token agreement vs the original model on unseen ordinary text

models.label: o60 (Claude Opus, 60 passes)
models.design: 10 new layers before layer 0: token detectors, 13 fixed-offset RoPE heads to align digits, a content head for zero-shot prompts, exact carry look-ahead, then a large write that forces each answer digit.

models.label: s60 (Claude Sonnet, 60 passes)
models.design: 13 inserted layers + 4 mirror layers that erase all scratch work; fixed-offset attention, carry look-ahead MLPs. Needs a newline before the first number, so zero-shot prompts fail.

trackA.takeaway: Exact computation can be written into a stock LLM with no training: o60 is exact on every hidden problem and leaves ordinary text essentially unchanged. Known flaw: it fires on any digits+digits=, even inside 1+2+3=.

trackD_helpdesk.title: Hand-written Next-Concept Model: help-desk bot
trackD_helpdesk.test: 448 hidden messages: unseen phrasings, names, ticket numbers and templates; exact reply required (14 intents + copied name and ticket number)
trackD_helpdesk.comparison: Earlier hand-written token-by-token transformers: 97-98% on the easier canned-reply version (no name/ticket copying).
trackD_helpdesk.caveat: Hidden names are common names; both agents wrote long name lists from their own knowledge, so the name score mostly measures list coverage.
trackD_helpdesk.takeaway: Both agents independently chose the same 2-level split: one plan code (intent x name? x ticket?), then all reply tokens in parallel. Coarse = concept, fine = words.

trackD_chat.title: Open-ended chat as a Next-Concept Model, with no lexicons and no training
trackD_chat.test: 40 tool-free Stage X dev cases (33 mechanically checked turns, incl. a 64-turn memory session). Blind test not run.

models.label: Round 1: nco60 (2 levels, no Qwen layers)
can: remembers and recalls facts the user gives

models.label: Round 2: ncd60 (4 levels with stated meanings, may reuse Qwen layers)
can: each of the 4 levels stays readable: act -> content word -> phrase skeleton -> tokens

trackD_chat.finding: ncd60 measured that the base Qwen's deep layers are not a usable knowledge store in this setup: token identity fades after layer ~20 and answers appear only at layers 22-24, unreliably, in chat format. Likely next step: the chat-trained Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and a direct knowledge port.
trackD_chat.baseline: Earlier hand-built 20M-param chatbots (Stage X): 14/46 and 21/54 on the fuller dev set including tool cases.

lessons: Exact, rule-based tasks (Pong, addition, slot copying) are where hand-written weights shine: perfect or near-perfect on hidden tests.
Language understanding is the bottleneck: without training or lexicons, meaning has to come from existing weights, and the base 0.5B model did not provide reliable knowledge.
Coarse-to-fine (NCM) makes the structure of a model easy to explain: agents independently converged on plan-then-words designs.
Infrastructure matters: a stale guard cache once made a perfect model look broken; every run now writes a live log.

pure_chat.title: Pure weight generation: an open-ended chat bot written from scratch (paper protocol)
pure_chat.protocol: The agent wrote one model file (a standard transformer, 11 layers, 293M params, no normalisation) whose code generates every weight from its own reasoning; no pretrained weights, no training, no local execution (audited). 100 forward passes (dev runs, its own conversations, probes). The only addition to the paper's protocol: example models to study. Snapshots frozen at passes 10, 30, 50, 100.
pure_chat.test: Blind: 38 new conversations / 114 turns written by an independent agent after the freeze (no harmful-request category); a separate blind judge graded every reply against its rubric, with replies anonymised and shuffled across models.
findings: The pure-weights transformer scored 45.6% of hidden turns acceptable, about 3x the earlier no-lexicon NCM chat models (12-17%).
Returns stopped at pass 30: the pass 30, 50 and 100 snapshots give byte-identical replies on all 114 hidden turns; later passes only tuned the agent's own test conversations.

Strong where knowledge can be written directly: general knowledge 11/17, memory 10/19, long session 11/20, uncertainty 5/7. Zero on instructions (0/10), creative writing (0/4) and the benign 'kill a process' question (0/2): templates do not compose new text.
Protocol lesson: 'continue until every pass is used' was met by re-running identical conversations; the harness now refuses identical requests on an unchanged model.
